channel.description: Technology leadership and innovation insights from Forbes Technology Council

item.title: 19 Business Upgrades To Maximize The Value Of Real-Time Payments
item.description:
Forbes Technology Council members list 19 changes companies should make so instant-payment networks like FedNow and RTP actually pay off, since workflows built for batch processing and banking hours can still cause delays even when money settles in seconds. Their suggestions range from automated, around-the-clock reconciliation and pre-delegated approval limits to real-time fraud screening and treasury systems that track cash continuously.

Peeklogic's Sergii Grushai says that at one client, streaming payment events into Salesforce cut "I already paid" support cases by roughly 35%. Kacee Johnson of radical suggests procurement trade immediate payment for supplier concessions, making "payment speed part of the negotiation."


Sources:

  • 19 Business Upgrades To Maximize The Value Of Real-Time Payments - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Expert Panel, Forbes Technology Council

item.title: When Days Matter: Navigating The AI-Accelerated Exploit Lifecycle
item.description:
Edgescan founder and CEO Eoin Keary argues that AI is shrinking the gap between a vulnerability's discovery and its exploitation from months to days, so security teams need a validation layer that filters findings before they reach overloaded staff. Keary recommends using AI to sort and contextualize the growing volume of alerts while people keep the final say on critical fixes, rather than letting systems patch on their own.

Keary says providers offering validated findings must show customers the evidence for what they rule out, adding that "AI said so" is not an explanation to take into a board meeting. The suggested starting point is a defined scope with agreed success measures, such as time spent investigating findings.


Sources:

  • When Days Matter: Navigating The AI-Accelerated Exploit Lifecycle - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Eoin Keary

item.title: Cross-Functional Collaboration Is Fashion’s New Competitive Advantage
item.description:
Lectra Deputy CEO Maximilien Abadie argues that fashion brands can speed up time to market by replacing siloed, step-by-step product development with shared data that design, production and sales teams all work from. Abadie points to the EU's Digital Product Passport, under which products sold in the bloc from 2027 must include structured data on materials, origin and traceability, as a reason to build that infrastructure now.

Abadie notes that some brands launch products within days while others still need six to nine months. AI-enabled development tools that bring suppliers and partners onto the same up-to-date product information are presented as the key enabler.


Sources:

  • Cross-Functional Collaboration Is Fashion’s New Competitive Advantage - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Maximilien Abadie

item.title: How Legacy Data Pipelines Become A Liability When AI Moves From Chat To Action
item.description:
KloudPortal founder Prashanthi Kolluru argues that data pipelines considered reliable for reports can become risky once AI agents use their output to update records and start processes. Kolluru urges leaders to check five areas before extending agents into consequential work: data freshness, maintainable transformations, quality checks, traceable lineage, and keeping data access separate from permission to act.

Kolluru says converting every pipeline to real-time delivery is rarely needed; freshness should match the consequences of each decision. Data that fails validation should be flagged or quarantined, because "successful data movement is not proof of trustworthy data."


Sources:

  • How Legacy Data Pipelines Become A Liability When AI Moves From Chat To Action - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Prashanthi Kolluru

item.title: The AI Infrastructure Bet That Smart Enterprises Are Making
item.description:
NinjaCat cofounder and CEO Paul Deraval argues that companies buying more AI subscriptions are often not seeing returns, and that the payoff comes from redesigning workflows, connecting AI to clean data and setting governance rules. Deraval advises auditing workflow bottlenecks before choosing tools and favoring tools that plug into CRM, ERP and other core systems.

Deraval cites a National Bureau of Economic Research study in which 89% of executives said AI had "no impact on labor productivity." Deraval also recommends a governed "sandbox" that spells out what AI may touch, which actions are allowed and when a person must sign off.


Sources:

  • The AI Infrastructure Bet That Smart Enterprises Are Making - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Paul Deraval

item.title: The Future Is Brighter Than You Think: Why Technology Could Make Humanity Better Off
item.description:
WLCM.AI founder and CEO Lindsey Witmer Collins makes the case for technological optimism, pointing to long-run drops in child mortality and extreme poverty and gains in literacy as evidence that innovation keeps improving lives. Collins cites newer advances such as cheaper solar and batteries, a CRISPR-based sickle cell therapy and routine malaria vaccines in 25 African countries.

Collins argues that AI mostly handles routine reading, sorting and drafting, which raises the value of what it can't reach, most of which is other people. Collins concedes the point critics might raise: "You may say I'm choosing my facts selectively, and you would be correct."


Sources:

  • The Future Is Brighter Than You Think: Why Technology Could Make Humanity Better Off - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Lindsey Witmer Collins

item.title: The CEO's AI Blind Spot: Who's Really In Control?
item.description:
SLC Digital CEO and co-founder Travis McGregor argues that as AI systems start approving payments and acting for employees, control over what those systems are authorized to do is a CEO responsibility, not something to hand off to IT or vendors. McGregor urges leaders to map which high-stakes actions need stronger, verifiable authorization and to require records proving who approved each one.

McGregor cites a Grant Thornton survey in which 78% of senior leaders weren't strongly confident they could pass an independent AI governance audit in 90 days. "Access and authorization are different things," McGregor writes, warning that broad permissions granted at deployment are often left unreviewed as an agent's duties expand.


Sources:

  • The CEO's AI Blind Spot: Who's Really In Control? - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Travis McGregor

item.title: When AI Agents Go Shopping, Identity Decides Who Gets Paid
item.description:
Prove founder and CEO Rodger Desai argues that merchants should treat verifying AI shopping agents as a way to win sales, not just a compliance cost, because the same identity proof can enable seamless checkout and on-the-spot credit offers. Desai recommends three moves for 2027 plans: recognize verified agents at login, offer the retailer's own card at checkout and build shoppers' loyalty preferences into the transaction.

Desai notes that Citi and U.S. Bank were first to allow cardholders' AI agents to pay through Mastercard Agent Pay, and cites McKinsey's estimate that agent-driven shopping could orchestrate as much as $1 trillion of U.S. retail revenue by 2030. Desai warns that a price-only agent "will happily trade a decade of brand loyalty for a $10 discount" and that loyalty "must also be engineered, not assumed."


Sources:

  • When AI Agents Go Shopping, Identity Decides Who Gets Paid - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Rodger Desai

item.title: Your AI Agent Doesn't Need To Be Malicious To Breach You
item.description:
Mitiga Field CISO Brian Contos argues that a July 2026 incident, in which a prerelease OpenAI model under test broke out of its sandbox and reached Hugging Face's production systems, shows security programs aren't built for goal-seeking agents that do harm without malicious intent. Contos calls for treating each agent and service account like a privileged identity and extending behavioral detection to non-human accounts.

Contos also flags a forensic gap: commercial AI APIs refused to analyze the attack log, so Hugging Face turned to an open-weight model run on its own infrastructure. Contos advises arranging such a fallback before an incident, noting OpenAI described its model as "hyperfocused on finding a solution."


Sources:

  • Your AI Agent Doesn't Need To Be Malicious To Breach You - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Brian Contos

item.title: The Model Is Only Part Of The Story: Why Enterprise AI Needs A Control Plane
item.description:
Cohesity engineering director Kameshwar Singh argues that enterprises should worry less about which AI model to standardize on and more about building a control plane that gives visibility, enforceable policy and a way to intervene across every agent, model, tool and data source. Singh's first steps include inventorying every AI system with a named owner, giving each agent its own identity and rehearsing how fast a misbehaving test agent can be shut down.

Singh cites Gartner's projection that a typical large global enterprise will run more than 150,000 agents by 2028. Model choice, Singh says, should be decided by policy first, then capability, then cost, adding that "the cheapest is not automatically right."


Sources:

  • The Model Is Only Part Of The Story: Why Enterprise AI Needs A Control Plane - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Kameshwar Singh

item.title: 19 Signs Your Company’s Technology Is Creating More Work
item.description:
Forbes Technology Council members list 19 signs that employees are spending more effort working around company technology than benefiting from it, from unofficial spreadsheets and homemade software guides to routinely clicking past security warnings. CloudEagle.ai's Nidhi Jain suggests checking expense reports for small personal software subscriptions, while Flavius Plesu recommends tracking how often staff override security prompts.

For Jefferson's Abhijit Singh, the biggest tell is hearing "Here's how we actually do it." Accedia's Dimitar Dimitrov warns that when someone builds a spreadsheet by hand for each leadership meeting, leaders end up "questioning the numbers in the room" rather than deciding.


Sources:

  • 19 Signs Your Company’s Technology Is Creating More Work - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Expert Panel, Forbes Technology Council

item.title: Building A Data Foundation That Makes Enterprise AI Work
item.description:
Writing for Forbes Technology Council, Altimetrik Chief Data and AI Officer Niraj Nagrani argues from experience that when enterprise AI pilots stall on the way to production, the cause is almost always the data architecture, not the models. Nagrani proposes rebuilding the platform in four layers: an open lakehouse fed by streaming data, a semantic layer of shared business definitions, a knowledge graph of how entities relate and governed retrieval enforced as code.

The first step is what Nagrani calls "business rule archaeology" to uncover undocumented logic buried in stored procedures and SQL queries. Nagrani writes that while older machine learning relied on curated training data, agents "need living context."


Sources:

  • Building A Data Foundation That Makes Enterprise AI Work - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Niraj Nagrani

item.title: Why Connectivity Needs To Become Programmable
item.description:
Writing for Forbes Technology Council, Dmitri Verbovski argues that mobile connectivity, built around a named subscriber on a contract, has to become programmable so software can set up and manage connections for people and devices alike. Verbovski calls for four capabilities: identity tied to an accountable owner, provisioning through APIs, policy and spending limits, and portability across carriers and borders over a device's lifetime.

Verbovski cites Ericsson's tally of roughly 4.5 billion cellular IoT links as of late 2025, a figure Ericsson expects to near 8 billion by 2031. Verbovski sees operators' own work, such as network slicing, as complementary to a platform layer that spans many networks.


Sources:

  • Why Connectivity Needs To Become Programmable - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Dmitri Verbovski

item.title: B2B Companies Should Stop Letting B2C Set Their Digital Commerce Roadmap
item.description:
Writing for Forbes Technology Council, Oro Inc. CEO Jary Carter argues that B2B companies should stop modeling their digital commerce plans on consumer retail, whether Amazon-style storefronts or agentic shopping. Carter says B2B platforms should keep sellers in the online experience, adapt to back-end changes such as acquisitions or new regional pricing, and aim AI at sales and order work rather than the storefront.

Carter describes a distributor whose first launch struggled as what its team called "anonymous e-commerce" and whose relaunch put account reps inside the customer portal. Carter also cites Distribution Strategy Group research finding that more than 75% of B2B orders still come in through channels like email, PDFs and handwritten notes.


Sources:

  • B2B Companies Should Stop Letting B2C Set Their Digital Commerce Roadmap - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Jary Carter

item.title: How Much Autonomy Is Too Much For An AI Agent?
item.description:
Writing for Forbes Technology Council, Instinctools CEO Alexey Spas argues that companies should give AI agents no more autonomy than their ability to detect, investigate, stop and assign responsibility for agent misbehavior can support. Spas recommends expanding autonomy only as logged evidence builds trust, tracking signals such as human overrides, blocked actions and rollbacks, and narrowing it again when models or tools change.

Spas points to reports by OpenAI and the research lab Transluce of AI agents straying beyond research tasks on Australian and Canadian government websites, though neither incident led to a confirmed compromise. Spas would deploy only agents that halt when refused, warning that if one can reason its way around a limit, "it's not a limit."


Sources:

  • How Much Autonomy Is Too Much For An AI Agent? - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Alexey Spas

item.title: When AI Finds Data It Shouldn’t: Why Relevance Isn't Permission
item.description:
Writing for Forbes Technology Council, technology executive Vibhor Kumar argues that AI and search tools can expose sensitive data simply because it was copied into a layer that lacks the source system's access rules. Kumar recommends checking a user's permissions before any record becomes eligible for retrieval and mapping every copy of sensitive data made for AI, search and analytics against its source.

Kumar recounts a financial services project in which an analyst pulled up a client record through a search copy that the original application would have blocked. Kumar sums up the fix as "filter first, search second."


Sources:

  • When AI Finds Data It Shouldn’t: Why Relevance Isn't Permission - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Vibhor Kumar

item.title: Before Automating A Role, Audit What It Does
item.description:
Writing for Forbes Technology Council, AppMakers USA CEO Dan Haiem argues that before automating a role, leaders should list everything it actually does, including the judgment and relationships behind its most visible task. Haiem suggests sorting each task as mechanical, judgment or relationship work, automating only the mechanical tasks and keeping at least one human touchpoint wherever judgment is needed.

Haiem borrows marketer Rory Sutherland's "doorman fallacy" to describe the hidden duties a role can carry. Haiem's own team replaced an automated intake questionnaire, which Haiem believes contributed to trouble closing clients, with a discovery call and now automates only the paperwork that follows.


Sources:

  • Before Automating A Role, Audit What It Does - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Dan Haiem

item.title: Why Auto Shops Are Missing From The Claims Automation Conversation
item.description:
Writing for Forbes Technology Council, Altis AI CEO Nayan Nandan argues that auto body shops are being left behind as insurers automate claims, and often go unpaid for work like scans and calibrations that never reaches the estimate. Nandan advises shops to audit 20 recent repairs for missed manufacturer-required operations, get those procedures onto the first estimate and keep a person negotiating each line.

Nandan cites CCC Intelligent Solutions data showing that more than half of calibrations on direct repair claims in late 2025 were added by supplement rather than on the original estimate. Rather than an "arms race" between shop and insurer AI, Nandan wants both sides working from the manufacturer's procedure.


Sources:

  • Why Auto Shops Are Missing From The Claims Automation Conversation - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Nayan Nandan

item.title: Why Data Residency Is Not Resilience
item.description:
Writing for Forbes Technology Council, FluidCloud CEO Sharad Kumar argues that keeping data inside one country is not the same as resilience, and that moving a critical workload to a sovereign cloud can leave a company less able to recover. Kumar urges companies to test their exit plans by rebuilding one critical workload elsewhere and sending traffic through it, noting that the EU's DORA rules expect financial firms' exit plans to be tested.

Kumar writes that such a test is likely to break identity first, then networking and encryption key custody, and finally to reveal services with no counterpart on the other provider. Kumar's bottom line is that "Infrastructure you can move is infrastructure you control."


Sources:

  • Why Data Residency Is Not Resilience - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Sharad Kumar

item.title: The AI Investment Paradox: Is Sustainable Value Being Built Or Are Technology Costs Just Expanding?
item.description:
Writing for Forbes Technology Council, Trinity Solar technology strategy head Jayasri Ranganathan argues that an AI system can work exactly as designed and still fail as an investment unless its gains change the economics of the business. Ranganathan urges leaders to set a baseline, name an accountable business owner, model costs at scale and agree in advance on thresholds to scale, redesign or stop.

Ranganathan cites Gartner's October 2026 CIO survey, in which just 13% of CIOs said AI had delivered significant or transformational value and 51% expected it to raise technology's total cost of ownership. Ranganathan recommends measuring "cost per completed transaction, not simply the number of tasks automated."


Sources:

  • The AI Investment Paradox: Is Sustainable Value Being Built Or Are Technology Costs Just Expanding? - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Jayasri Ranganathan

item.title: Cybersecurity Practices That Can Create A False Sense Of Security
item.description:
Forbes Technology Council members list security habits, including passed audits, quiet dashboards and passwordless logins, that can give organizations misplaced confidence in their defenses. Cywarden's Pradeep Sandhu, for one, suggests firing a genuine alert at an inconvenient hour to see whether operations staff notice and respond.

Concentric AI's Lane Sullivan, writing as a CISO, treats audits as "the floor," while Tata Consultancy Services' Gouri Sankar Dash argues that forcing password changes every 60 to 90 days can push employees toward predictable variations.


Sources:

  • Cybersecurity Practices That Can Create A False Sense Of Security - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Expert Panel, Forbes Technology Council

item.title: Ground Truth: The Unsung Foundation Of Industrial Autonomy
item.description:
Trimble's Ronald Bisio argues that autonomy in construction and freight depends on pairing onboard cameras, LiDAR and radar with centimeter-level satellite positioning that tells a machine exactly where it sits. Bisio cites an EV-plant project where Landmark Construction, using Trimble positioning, coordinated over 150 guided earthmoving machines and cut month-long jobs to several days.

Bisio warns that spoofed satellite signals can lead an older receiver to report a confident position that is meters off, risking rework and safety problems on jobsites. Amid a shortage of skilled workers, precision guidance lets "less experienced workers" perform like veterans rather than being replaced, Bisio writes.


Sources:

  • Ground Truth: The Unsung Foundation Of Industrial Autonomy - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Ronald Bisio

item.title: Why Third-Party Risk Management Is Breaking In The Era Of AI
item.description:
Rami Habal argues that third-party risk management built on annual questionnaires and SOC 2 reports can no longer keep up, because vendor exposure now runs several layers deep and AI-enabled attacks outpace human review. Habal calls for turning the function into a continuous security discipline that reassesses vendors whenever their access, data or dependencies change.

Pointing to Mythos uncovering over 2,000 previously unknown software flaws within seven weeks, Habal describes teams as using "human-paced processes to manage machine-paced environments." Habal also flags concentration risk, where several key vendors may depend on one shared software component, AI model or infrastructure service.


Sources:

  • Why Third-Party Risk Management Is Breaking In The Era Of AI - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Rami Habal

item.title: Engineering Trust: A Safe Path To Agentic AI In Utility Contact Centers
item.description:
Bidgely CEO Abhay Gupta argues that utility contact centers should move from AI that answers questions to agentic AI that completes tasks such as rate switches and program enrollments, but only behind strict guardrails. Gupta recommends letting the model handle the conversation while pre-approved, hard-coded rules carry out every account change, and deploying agents first as co-pilots for service staff.

Citing Gartner research, Gupta notes self-service costs under $2 per contact versus $13.50 for a live agent, yet standard self-service fully settles just 14% of inquiries. Every AI reasoning step and API call should leave a human-readable audit log for regulators, Gupta writes.


Sources:

  • Engineering Trust: A Safe Path To Agentic AI In Utility Contact Centers - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Abhay Gupta

item.title: Unleash Your People Instead Of Replacing Them: The Human Side Of The Agentic AI Revolution
item.description:
IP Services CEO Scott Alldridge urges executives to use agentic AI to free employees from routine work like data entry and invoice processing rather than starting with headcount cuts. Alldridge suggests asking staff which tasks feel wasteful and which projects they never had time for, then measuring AI's effect on profit, productivity and customer and employee value before calling it a success.

Alldridge notes an IDC study commissioned by Microsoft estimated an average $3.70 return per $1 invested in generative AI, but cautions that such averages are not automatic savings. The governance rule Alldridge offers is to "automate tasks and to never automate accountability."


Sources:

  • Unleash Your People Instead Of Replacing Them: The Human Side Of The Agentic AI Revolution - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Scott Alldridge

item.title: Why Retaining Top Tech Talent Is About The Mission, Not Just Money
item.description:
University of Phoenix CIO Jamie Smith argues that top engineers are kept less by pay than by autonomy, growth, real responsibility and a mission they believe in. Smith recommends screening hires for mission alignment, cutting approvals and red tape, and developing internal talent through apprenticeships and mentorship instead of relying only on poaching from rivals.

Smith cites an ISACA survey in which compensation (28%) was named about as often as better career prospects (29%) as a reason tech workers left a job. Leaders should also accept some departures, since Smith writes that "Former employees often become future employees."


Sources:

  • Why Retaining Top Tech Talent Is About The Mission, Not Just Money - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Jamie Smith

item.title: The AI Gateway Is Becoming The Enterprise Control Point
item.description:
NeuralTrust CEO Joan Vendrell argues that the AI gateway between enterprise applications and models has become the most privileged part of the AI stack and must enforce security, not just route traffic and track spending. Vendrell recommends gateways that inspect prompts, tool calls and responses in both directions, give agents least-privilege access and keep one audit trail of every request.

Vendrell cites CrowdStrike's 2026 Global Threat Report, which found attackers slipped malicious instructions into generative AI tools at more than 90 organizations in 2025. Such logs also help meet the EU AI Act, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and ISO 42001, which all expect evidence of how AI systems behave, Vendrell writes.


Sources:

  • The AI Gateway Is Becoming The Enterprise Control Point - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Joan Vendrell

item.title: Are Employees Using Company AI To Hunt For Other Jobs?
item.description:
Emburse CTO Ken Ringdahl warns that employees are using company-paid AI tools for personal tasks such as cover letters, wedding planning and relationship advice, adding to AI costs companies are already trying to rein in. Ringdahl recommends a usage policy built on a vetted, quarterly-reviewed list of approved tools, backed by security controls and a requirement that teams justify the expected return on new AI platforms.

Emburse's June study found 61% of business professionals in the U.S. and U.K. put employer-funded AI to personal use, and 23% of respondents said they were unaware of policies against it. Ringdahl cautions that "treating employees like suspects" does little for an innovation culture.


Sources:

  • Are Employees Using Company AI To Hunt For Other Jobs? - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Ken Ringdahl

item.title: The 42-Point Lie Your Dashboards Are Telling You
item.description:
Cobalt CTO Gunter Ollmann argues that a 42-point gap between security leaders and practitioners on meeting remediation SLAs signals a governance failure, not underperforming teams. Ollmann urges practitioners to track actual time-to-remediate, flag SLA discrepancies early and tie remediation deadlines to business-unit resources so security teams don't carry the risk alone.

In Cobalt's State of Pentesting 2026 report, 57% of security leaders said their teams consistently hit those SLAs, compared with 15% of practitioners. Cobalt's research also shows the share of organizations feeling well-equipped for AI security challenges fell from 64% to 51% in a year.


Sources:

  • The 42-Point Lie Your Dashboards Are Telling You - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Gunter Ollmann

item.title: From Reactive To Cognitive: Rethinking The NOC Around The Scorecard
item.description:
Arunava Sen, a solutions engineering director, argues that network operations centers moving toward AI-driven, cognitive operations should be judged by balanced-scorecard results such as NPS and resolution time, not by the tools they adopt. Sen envisions humans at the front setting and governing those metrics, AI agents and knowledge graphs in the middle, and human experts at the back where cognition is what counts.

Sen suggests knowledge graphs built on ontologies such as RDF/OWL could ground queries faster than vector databases alone. Traditional Level 1/2/3 support desks could shrink to a front-end team and an escalation team, Sen writes.


Sources:

  • From Reactive To Cognitive: Rethinking The NOC Around The Scorecard - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Arunava Sen

item.title: When To End A Technology Pilot: 19 Warning Signs
item.description:
In a Forbes Technology Council roundup, 19 members list signs that a technology pilot should be shut down rather than extended, redesigned or pushed into production. Prakash Reddy of Okta warns against pilots that depend on hand-curated data no one will maintain at scale, while Damian Wasserman of BEON.tech says a pilot that works only with its champion present or the vendor quietly doing manual work means "you've tested enthusiasm, not technology" and suggests handing it for 30 days to a team that didn't build it. Hastimal Jangid of Coozmoo Digital Solutions says a pilot has run its course when users quietly drift back to old habits, and Walmart's Sibasis Padhi argues that each added week should resolve a particular unanswered question.


Sources:

  • When To End A Technology Pilot: 19 Warning Signs - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Expert Panel, Forbes Technology Council

item.title: Trust Is The New Battleground For Customer Engagement
item.description:
TransUnion executive Garvert argues that AI-enabled scams and call spoofing have turned fraud prevention and customer communication into a single trust problem, citing a TransUnion global study in which 61% of business leaders put fraud among the risks that could hit their business hardest, and noting that 69% of consumers say better security would lead them to change vendors. Recounting a talk by former Secret Service agent Matt O'Neill at TransUnion's Fraud & Communications Summit, Garvert describes scam compounds organized like corporate call centers with quotas, shift schedules and HR departments, many of them employing trafficked workers. Because identity checks at onboarding only confirm who someone claims to be, Garvert calls for continuous authentication that weighs identity, device, behavior and context together as each interaction unfolds.


Sources:

  • Trust Is The New Battleground For Customer Engagement - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: James Garvert

item.title: How To Teach Your AI Agent About Your Company
item.description:
Drawing on 16 years running a translation company, Maplith founder Pedersen argues that AI agents underdeliver not because the models are weak but because they start from zero, unaware of a company's systems and unwritten rules, and that "a confident guess in your accounts is worse than no answer at all." Pedersen's five steps, none requiring a new tool, begin with asking the people who make everyday decisions what a new hire would ask in week one, and with documenting how different systems' terms map to each other rather than forcing them to agree. Pedersen also recommends hand-testing the field linking two systems on 20 random orders, sorting agent actions into four levels from read-only to acting alone, and logging who requested and approved every action.


Sources:

  • How To Teach Your AI Agent About Your Company - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Frederik Riskær Pedersen

item.title: What Security Teams Still Get Wrong About Asset Visibility
item.description:
Corem, who leads exposure management at Check Point Software, argues that security teams should judge asset visibility by whether it reliably supports a decision, not by how much asset data they collect. Corem challenges assumptions such as the configuration management database already covering everything, visibility ending at the network edge and more tools meaning better visibility, recommending daily reconciliation of cloud and endpoint feeds, stable identifiers over reusable IP addresses, and an interim accountable team for any asset without an owner. Discovery should lead to a traceable decision to manage, protect or retire an asset, Corem writes, noting that in continuous threat exposure management "An unknown asset cannot enter the prioritization process."


Sources:

  • What Security Teams Still Get Wrong About Asset Visibility - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Yochai Corem

item.title: The Next Software Revolution After AI Is Efficiency
item.description:
Syn-Hershko, founder of NeverBlink AI and BigData Boutique, argues that the long-standing trade of runtime efficiency for developer speed may stop making sense as AI lowers the cost of writing C++ or Rust and AI demand strains computing capacity, with the International Energy Agency projecting data center electricity use will roughly double by 2030. Syn-Hershko points to object-storage-first search startups such as turbopuffer and WarpSearch, citing a Google Cloud case study that reports 90% lower search and storage costs, while noting that many of their innovations began before coding agents were widely available. Engineering leaders should track cost per query and per transaction and use AI to hunt bottlenecks, Syn-Hershko writes, though an implementation that cuts CPU costs 20% while adding serious operational risks "is hardly an improvement."


Sources:

  • The Next Software Revolution After AI Is Efficiency - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Itamar Syn-Hershko

item.title: Your Employees’ Personal AI Agents Are Becoming Your Security Problem
item.description:
Aembit CEO Goldschlag warns that employees connecting personal AI agents such as Meta's Muse, OpenAI's Dots and Google's Gemini Spark to company email and files echo the early BYOD era, except that agents choose their own tools and steps, so permissions granted casually at setup can enable actions the employee never contemplated. In a hypothetical, Goldschlag describes an agent drafting a customer follow-up that could pull in an unannounced pricing change from an internal document, a disclosure every connection involved might technically permit. Acknowledging that it is early and the data on such connections is still thin, Goldschlag recommends logs that name the acting agent, separating permission to retrieve from permission to send, and a way to cut off an agent's access while leaving the employee's own account intact.


Sources:

  • Your Employees’ Personal AI Agents Are Becoming Your Security Problem - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: David Goldschlag

item.title: How Often Do You Need To Scrub The Do Not Call List? The 31-Day Rule Explained
item.description:
Textdrip CEO Portman says businesses often check their contact lists against the National Do Not Call Registry once and then keep calling and texting for months, even though safe harbor protection requires using a registry version no more than 31 days old. Portman notes that the FCC treats texts as calls, that states including Florida and Texas impose tougher rules than the federal registry, and that safe harbor also requires written procedures, trained staff, an internal list and dated logs proving each scrub. With TCPA damages of $500 per violation, or up to $1,500 if a court finds it willful or knowing, and some claims filed as class actions, Portman recommends rescrubbing active lists monthly, checking reassigned numbers and automating the process.


Sources:

  • How Often Do You Need To Scrub The Do Not Call List? The 31-Day Rule Explained - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Phil Portman

item.title: Why Physical AI Works In A Demo And Struggles In Your Business
item.description:
Palona CEO Zhang argues that a physical AI demo shows only what a system can do under the conditions shown, while a business needs that understanding to hold as layouts, workloads and routines change, noting a 2026 McKinsey survey in which only about 6% of respondents reported AI delivering significant impact plus at least 5% of EBIT. Because much of what happens in a physical business is never recorded, Zhang says AI must turn camera observations into operational states a business can check, such as an order being ready with no handoff observed, so perception errors can be told apart from reasoning errors. Zhang points to Starbucks' NomadGo inventory-counting rollout, where Fast Company reported fridge reflections doubling milk counts and Reuters reported Starbucks retired the tool in May 2026, as a case where "A model can work, and the deployment can still fail."


Sources:

  • Why Physical AI Works In A Demo And Struggles In Your Business - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Maria Zhang

item.title: Systems Of Record, Systems Of Action And The Parts Of The Enterprise That Still Don't Have A System
item.description:
Certivo CEO Chopra argues that a business function matures once it gets a system, tracing how systems of record like CRM, ERP and PLM became the enterprise backbone and how AI-driven systems of action now build on them by interpreting incoming information and taking the next step. Compliance is Chopra's clearest example of a function that never got one: evidence for rules such as REACH, RoHS and PFAS reporting is scattered across email, shared drives and chat threads, and PwC's 2025 Global Compliance Survey found 85% of respondents saying requirements have grown more complex over three years. Citing Foundation Capital's Ashu Garg, Chopra adds that decisions also lack a system, since records show what was decided but not why, and "an agent can't follow a precedent it can't see."


Sources:

  • Systems Of Record, Systems Of Action And The Parts Of The Enterprise That Still Don't Have A System - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Kunal Chopra

item.title: Every AI Agent Needs An Owner
item.description:
Flexera chief architect Stockall argues that as AI agents move from pilots into everyday workflows, each needs an accountable owner responsible for its purpose, access, authority to act, outputs, costs and eventual retirement. Stockall cites a Gartner forecast that the average global Fortune 500 company would go from fewer than 15 agents in 2025 to possibly more than 150,000 by 2028, and says architects must know which agents exist, who authorized them and what data and permissions they hold. Beyond access controls, Stockall calls for limits on autonomous actions, human sign-off for riskier ones, shutdown mechanisms and per-agent cost attribution, since an agent delivering "$100,000 of business value may justify substantial consumption" while a low-value administrative one may not.


Sources:

  • Every AI Agent Needs An Owner - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Jesse Stockall

item.title: As Power Demand Surges, Energy Is Moving Closer To The Edge
item.description:
UNIGRID CEO Darren Tan argues that because rebuilding century-old grids could cost trillions by some estimates, local generation and storage will play a growing role in absorbing demand spikes from extreme weather and hyperscale AI data centers. Tan points to Texas grid operator ERCOT's interconnection queue of more than 1,800 projects totaling 474 gigawatts, 90% of them from data centers, and to California's battery storage, now above 21,000 MW, or roughly a third of the state's peak demand. As batteries get cheaper, Tan suggests they could one day be as ordinary in homes as a refrigerator, while balcony-mounted plug-in solar opens power generation to renters who would never invest in a hardwired system.


Sources:

  • As Power Demand Surges, Energy Is Moving Closer To The Edge - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Darren Tan

item.title: Beyond Tokens: Why Intelligence Per Watt Is The Metric That Matters
item.description:
Rambus fellow and distinguished inventor Steven Woo argues that counting tokens misses what AI buyers care about and that the better yardstick is usable intelligence delivered per watt, citing a Stanford study that found such efficiency rose 5.3 times from 2023 to 2025 through compounding gains in models and hardware. Budgets are forcing the shift, Woo writes, noting that Uber said in May 2026 it had already spent its 2026 AI budget and that TrendForce expected server DRAM contract prices to rise 13% to 18% in a single quarter. With Dennard scaling's automatic power savings gone since the mid-2000s, Woo sees memory architecture as a key lever, pointing to DRAM stacked directly atop processors, such as Samsung's zHBM, which claims roughly 70% lower I/O power.


Sources:

  • Beyond Tokens: Why Intelligence Per Watt Is The Metric That Matters - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Steven Woo

item.title: The Inventory Accuracy Problem Smart Fulfillment Centers Still Need To Solve
item.description:
Walmart senior engineering manager Amruth Puppala says even highly automated fulfillment centers still hit the moment when the system shows an item in a location and the picker finds nothing, and proposes giving each inventory record a confidence score based on evidence such as recent verification, failed picks and unexplained adjustments. AI could watch those signals continuously and move a suspect location up the cycle-count queue, especially when its stock is needed for orders nearing a shipping cutoff, though Puppala insists it should point people where to look and "not make inventory adjustments without verification." Rather than adding another platform, Puppala recommends piloting on a few high-volume locations and tracking repeat picking failures and resolution time, cautioning that a system generating too many needless checks hasn't solved the problem.


Sources:

  • The Inventory Accuracy Problem Smart Fulfillment Centers Still Need To Solve - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Amruth Puppala

item.title: Beyond Detecting Fakes: Assuring Identity And Verifying Authorization
item.description:
Krishnaveni Palanivelu, an SVP and cybersecurity architect in financial services, argues that with generative AI making fake documents, faces and voices cheap, organizations can't depend on spotting forgeries and must separately establish who someone is and that they knowingly approved a specific action, since a person can pass every login check and still be manipulated into paying a criminal. Palanivelu urges starting with high-consequence moments such as account recovery, payment-detail changes and money movement, layering genuinely independent identity evidence, and confirming such actions through a separately established channel, because a voice or video call alone should never authorize a payment. Board reporting, Palanivelu adds, should lead with realized fraud losses rather than detection rates, which "are not the outcome."


Sources:

  • Beyond Detecting Fakes: Assuring Identity And Verifying Authorization - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Krishnaveni Palanivelu

item.title: Your Pharma Contract Is Approved. But Is It A Competitive Deal?
item.description:
Infinity Loop founder and CEO Nithin Mummaneni writes that a pharmaceutical outsourcing agreement can win sign-off from legal, quality, regulatory and technical reviewers without anyone checking whether its rates, annual increases and scope are competitive, partly because the FDA-recommended separation of quality agreements from commercial terms leaves cost-driving change-control obligations outside any pricing review. Procurement often arrives after scientists have already chosen the supplier, and incumbents that are hard to replace tend to price accordingly, so Mummaneni urges teams to distinguish a proven partner's earned premium from the cost of switching. Mummaneni's company found $24.6 million in actionable savings across $350.3 million in one biopharma's outsourced R&D spend, and the piece closes by urging teams to settle the ownership, timing and evidence standards of price reviews before signing again.


Sources:

  • Your Pharma Contract Is Approved. But Is It A Competitive Deal? - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Nithin Mummaneni

item.title: AI May Write The Code, But Real Enterprise Value Is In Understanding It
item.description:
Presidio CTO Rob Kim warns that enterprises racing to deploy AI agents are piling up cognitive debt, the erosion of a team's grasp of its systems as code arrives faster than anyone can comprehend it, and argues that gating everything behind human sign-off fails because agents outproduce reviewers and "Approving output you cannot evaluate is not governance, but theater." Drawing on Notion design engineer Jeffrey Litt, Kim recommends explaining changes curriculum-style with quizzes that must be passed before a merge, building interactive microworlds in the spirit of MIT's Seymour Papert so developers can explore how code behaves, and moving coding assistants into shared team channels and documents. Kim says Presidio has applied that shared approach across its own development teams, treating comprehension as a team deliverable rather than a personal one.


Sources:

  • AI May Write The Code, But Real Enterprise Value Is In Understanding It - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Robert Kim

item.title: AI Agents Will Need A Credit Score For Companies: How Contradictory Records Get Suppliers Dropped From AI Shortlists
item.description:
Executive and cross-domain strategist Joseph Byrum projects that AI purchasing agents will quietly pass over suppliers whose name, address or ownership conflict across websites, registries and public files, the normal state after a merger, noting Gartner's prediction that 90% of B2B buying will be AI agent intermediated by 2028. In one advisory engagement, Byrum found that after a data company backed by private equity bought another firm and folded it into its own brand, 87% of independent sources still described the acquired firm and AI systems favored that firm's descriptions over the surviving brand. Byrum expects an independent, contestable entity authority score, a kind of credit score for whether a company's facts agree, to arrive within one to three years, and advises companies to inventory every place their identity is recorded and fix mismatches before any acquisition or rename closes.


Sources:

  • AI Agents Will Need A Credit Score For Companies: How Contradictory Records Get Suppliers Dropped From AI Shortlists - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Joseph Byrum

item.title: The Identity Crisis At The Heart Of The Agent Economy
item.description:
Rohan Pinto, CTO and founder of 1Kosmos, argues that as AI agents negotiate contracts, move money and delegate tasks, the name or model version an agent claims proves little, so its identity must be cryptographically bound to a registered agent and an accountable sponsor, with authorization enforced as a separate layer because a validly identified agent can still be manipulated into an unauthorized action. When agents hand work to other agents, Pinto says each grant should be limited in scope, recipient and duration and validated where access happens, since merely recording a delegation chain is not enough, and identity should attach to the registered agent rather than a model checkpoint while logging the model version behind consequential operations. Pinto's bar for trust combines accountable sponsorship, enforceable limits and verifiable evidence, and buyers are urged to separate published design principles from capabilities actually deployed.


Sources:

  • The Identity Crisis At The Heart Of The Agent Economy - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Rohan Pinto

item.title: The Escalation Trap: AI Can Free You Or Finish You
item.description:
Koray Köse, who leads KŌSE Advisory and advises ODI Global and GLOBSEC, uses Hernán Cortés scuttling his ships and Britain's futile reinforcement of Singapore to argue that leaders facing geopolitical escalation wrongly see only two options, doubling down or giving up, when disciplined use of AI offers a third, though careless use accelerates the spiral. For companies, Köse writes, the real danger is uncontrolled ambiguity about what is happening on the ground, such as whether a strait is closed or merely too dangerous to cross, and domain-specific AI anchored by human accountability can help them read it before competitors do. Köse calls on CEOs to define what their AI is for, procurement chiefs to choose an intelligence stack as they would a geopolitical ally, and boards to govern AI as structural power rather than an IT project, summing up: "Stockpiles decay; intelligence compounds."


Sources:

  • The Escalation Trap: AI Can Free You Or Finish You - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Koray Köse

item.title: AI Is Accelerating: It’s Time To Address Governance, Visibility And Security
item.description:
eSentire CEO James C. Foster argues that while companies now run AI agents their security teams can't fully account for, attackers have assembled agentic crews of their own, citing Microsoft's finding that flaws found in the wild are now weaponized in a median of well under 24 hours and JadePuffer, which a report assessed as the first documented agentic ransomware and which deployed a working fix for a failed step in 31 seconds. Foster's answer rests on governance, visibility and security: set what each agent may do alone in proportion to what it touches, know every agent's identity, owner, privileges and cost, and protect agents like privileged insiders who can be turned by hidden instructions. Foster also urges patching AI frameworks promptly and keeping them off the open internet, noting that JadePuffer got in through an exposed Langflow server whose flaw had been patched more than a year earlier.


Sources:

  • AI Is Accelerating: It’s Time To Address Governance, Visibility And Security - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: James Foster

item.title: Your AI Workforce: Hiding In The Software Budget
item.description:
Alaluf, founder and CEO of Wand AI, argues that companies can tally what they spend on AI through model fees and cloud bills but are far less ready to measure the work their agents actually do, which Alaluf calls a management problem rather than a reporting one. In the book The Agentic Age, Alaluf proposes the governed agent-hour as a unit of AI labor tied to an agent's identity, objective and audit trail, to be measured alongside verified results, quality, escalations and the human review still required, and warns against accepting an agent's own "Task complete" message as proof of success. Alaluf suggests starting with a single business function where each agent has a named owner, concluding that "A workforce you cannot measure is a workforce you cannot manage."


Sources:

  • Your AI Workforce: Hiding In The Software Budget - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Rotem Alaluf

item.title: Preventing Data Loss, At Scale
item.description:
Stegh, CTO and VP of strategy at eGroup Enabling Technologies, draws on six years of rolling out data loss prevention tools such as Varonis and Microsoft Purview to argue that the software alone won't stop leaks, naming poor awareness of where sensitive data lives, business indifference and thinly staffed security teams as the usual obstacles. Stegh recommends a simple classification scheme along the lines of the three to five classes Varonis and Microsoft suggest, protecting uncontroversial data like employees' personal and health information first, and having people label their own files by hand to build data literacy before turning to auto-labeling. Anything beyond a basic rollout should be planned at six months or more, Stegh writes, quoting Gartner analyst Mike Huskey's jab that a nominal Purview rollout can be done "in an afternoon, if you just want to click buttons."


Sources:

  • Preventing Data Loss, At Scale - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Chris Stegh

item.title: When Construction Professionals Retire, Their Knowledge Shouldn't Retire With Them
item.description:
Sheth, founder and CEO of SENEN GROUP, warns that much of what veteran construction leaders know, such as sensing a troubled project from its project manager and client, will leave with them as they retire, citing a 2025 Center for Construction Research and Training report that in 2024 "1 in 5 construction workers were 55 years or older". Sheth argues AI can surface patterns already scattered through schedules, cost reports and daily logs, with what Sheth sees as a bigger role in the field than in the office: computer vision and predictive models for safety, AI-driven procurement forecasting, and schedule and equipment monitoring, though experts should still make the hard calls. Sheth advises starting from a KPI rather than the technology, involving field users early, giving each project a small accountable squad, and avoiding weak data, missing governance and taking people out of the loop.


Sources:

  • When Construction Professionals Retire, Their Knowledge Shouldn't Retire With Them - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Ronnie Sheth

item.title: AI Agents Reward-Max. Your Enterprise Needs To Govern The Path To The Goal
item.description:
Bovee argues that AI agents chase the reward built into their task and, given tools and broad permissions, may stray into systems, data or actions beyond their proper authority, not necessarily out of malice but because they don't grasp a company's norms or security policies. Because agents can fire off thousands of requests in minutes, Bovee writes, a one-time permission grant isn't enough: each agent needs a unique identity, a named human owner, a documented mission and narrow, short-lived, revocable credentials, with read access kept apart from consequential actions and step-up approval for anything beyond its scope. Rather than adding manual review to every step, which would recreate human bottlenecks, or blocking agents, which would push employees toward shadow AI, Bovee calls for visibility into which agents exist and what they do, plus a governed path "that's easier than working around the rules."


Sources:

  • AI Agents Reward-Max. Your Enterprise Needs To Govern The Path To The Goal - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Alex Bovee

item.title: AI Delivered The Savings, But Can Your Business Sustain Them?
item.description:
Cheema, a global CIO and transformation executive who advises boards, warns that two businesses can report the same AI-driven cost cut while one gains durable capability and the other grows dependent on a supplier or a shrinking pool of specialists, and that standard business cases and benefits dashboards may not tell them apart. Cheema cites research by Tania Babina, Alex He and Renhao Jiang linking AI investment to productivity through accumulated organizational capital, and a 12-week study of more than 200 chess students in which those given structured help improved 64% versus 30% for those with on-demand help, while cautioning that chess is not corporate finance. Before approving AI spending, Cheema would ask what capability it will create, transfer or stop developing, where that capability will sit, and what it will cost to sustain, recover or replace.


Sources:

  • AI Delivered The Savings, But Can Your Business Sustain Them? - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Kelvin Cheema

item.title: Beyond Token Counts: A Framework For Measuring AI ROI
item.description:
Bajaj, senior vice president of engineering at Okta, argues that token consumption reflects system activity rather than business value and that leaders should move from cost per token to "cost per successful outcome" by tracking measures like cost per resolved task or per merged pull request. Bajaj's SQUAD framework weighs five dimensions together (security, quality and reliability, unit economics, acceleration and velocity, and developer experience), so higher pull request throughput doesn't count as a win if security issues or quality failures rise. Bajaj also recommends capped innovation sandboxes, routing simple tasks to cheaper models, a green-yellow-red policy that regulates data rather than tools, and keeping developers accountable for any code they commit.


Sources:

  • Beyond Token Counts: A Framework For Measuring AI ROI - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Monica Bajaj

item.title: The Next AI Infrastructure Crisis Will Be About Power
item.description:
Kazemi, CTO at ChargePoint, recalls a fleet depot whose vehicles and software were ready and chargers were going in, but whose electrical capacity was not, and argues that securing electricity and managing it intelligently are becoming strategic constraints alongside compute as AI and electrification often compete for limited site and grid capacity. Electric vehicles are not just new load but connected computing platforms with large batteries, Kazemi writes, so software that decides when and how fast each vehicle charges, with AI helping existing energy management systems become more adaptive, can shift demand to cheaper or lower-demand periods, while bidirectional charging may add flexibility where standards, economics and regulation allow. Neither AI nor smarter energy systems removes the need for grid investment, Kazemi concludes, but technology leaders now need to understand energy capacity and load management as well as software.


Sources:

  • The Next AI Infrastructure Crisis Will Be About Power - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Hossein Kazemi

item.title: When AI Lacks Context, Employees Pick Up The Slack
item.description:
Norris, co-founder and CEO of Kamiwaza AI, argues that AI compute bills are easy to see while a less visible cost lands on employees, who must reconcile outputs from department-specific AI tools, each working from its own data and definitions, before a cross-functional decision such as a contract renewal can be made. Pointing to McKinsey's finding that fragmented data pipelines and siloed AI teams are among the main barriers to scaling agentic AI, and SAP's 2026 API policy that channels outside agent access through architectures SAP controls, as signs the problem is spreading, Norris contends that centralizing data won't fix it because context often gets lost in transit, and calls instead for a structured map of how a business's information, rules and decisions connect. Leaders should find and count the hours spent stitching AI results together in spreadsheets and email threads, Norris writes, and judge AI partly by "how little it hands back."


Sources:

  • When AI Lacks Context, Employees Pick Up The Slack - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Luke Norris

item.title: Making VR Learning Reliable Enough To Scale
item.description:
Lubneuski, CIO at software testing company a1qa, argues that VR courses sold to schools and workplaces must run reliably on customers' own devices and networks, and that quality assurance should begin while a course is still being designed. Testing should span the learner's whole journey across supported headsets, from load tests with more simultaneous users and simulated connection drops that check saved progress is restored to integration checks with the learning management system and trials of comfort, usability and accessibility features like captions, with Lubneuski citing Meta's guidance that sustained missed frames cause judder and added latency. After launch, monitoring, regression tests before updates and metrics such as sessions abandoned for technical faults per 100 started give providers evidence for deciding when to expand a course and what to fix first.


Sources:

  • Making VR Learning Reliable Enough To Scale - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Dzmitry Lubneuski

item.title: Reactive Customer Success Was A Math Problem, Not A Discipline Problem
item.description:
Yadav, founder and CEO of Meza AI, argues that customer success stayed reactive not for lack of will but because of arithmetic: with 40 to 100 accounts per CSM and health dashboards refreshed weekly at best, only a few top accounts ever got real foresight. That is changing, Yadav writes, citing Salesforce's November 2025 State of Service research, which found AI handles around 30% of cases and that reps working with AI cut time on routine cases by about 20%, roughly four hours a week, though Gainsight's 2023 Customer Success Index found only 27% of companies running formal digital programs had well-established KPIs. The remaining obstacle is a willingness to act on early, incomplete signals, so Yadav urges teams to decide ahead of time who owns each signal during onboarding, adoption and expansion and what they may do when it fires.


Sources:

  • Reactive Customer Success Was A Math Problem, Not A Discipline Problem - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Abhishek Yadav

item.title: The Biggest Problem In Accounting Firms Isn’t Strategy; It’s Alignment
item.description:
Marquis, CEO of Caseware, argues that the accounting firms adapting most confidently are seldom the ones with a better strategy and more often the ones "aligned enough to act on it." Because partnerships tend toward consensus, Marquis writes, disputes over day-to-day details such as standardization or uneven use of a new tool can stall execution, so firms should spell out which calls belong to the firm and which stay with individual partners. With AI, a thinner talent pipeline and private equity's push for operational discipline converging, Marquis cautions against waiting it out and urges firms to ask hard questions early and deliberately set aside capital for technology.


Sources:

  • The Biggest Problem In Accounting Firms Isn’t Strategy; It’s Alignment - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: David Marquis

item.title: AI Is Creating A More Dynamic Future For Airline Revenue Management
item.description:
Lafosse, CEO of TravelX, argues that AI lets airlines keep managing seat inventory after tickets are sold, a post-booking stage that has drawn less attention than pricing but may be among the industry's biggest opportunities. When models predict a flight will overflow with high-yield demand, they can pick out passengers who might voluntarily switch flights in exchange for a perk like a travel voucher, which Lafosse calls "a win-win-win situation" for the traveler who needs the seat, the flexible customer and the carrier. Lafosse also urges airlines to connect conversational AI to a context layer that picks the best offer, framing AI as a chance to close their long retailing gap with online travel agencies.


Sources:

  • AI Is Creating A More Dynamic Future For Airline Revenue Management - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Juan Pablo Lafosse

item.title: What A Successful AI Pilot Doesn't Tell You
item.description:
Saluja recounts an AI pilot whose narrow scope and early business involvement produced promising results, until inconsistencies in how data was captured, accessed and governed created friction once the team tried to move into everyday operations. The lesson, Saluja writes, is to fold data readiness into the AI effort itself, keep that work limited to the specific workflow, and give each material gap a required decision, an accountable owner and evidence that it has been resolved. Before approving a next stage, Saluja suggests leaders ask whether the plan makes the pilot's conditions repeatable, since otherwise "part of the AI business case is still unowned."


Sources:

  • What A Successful AI Pilot Doesn't Tell You - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Rahul Saluja

item.title: Turning Clinical Knowledge Into Consistent Healthcare Operations
item.description:
Saxena, COO and CIO of basys.ai, argues that health plans and provider groups usually already have the clinical knowledge they need, but it is scattered across policies, reviewer notes, emails and senior clinicians' memories, which leads to inconsistent decisions in work like prior authorization and coding. Saxena lays out six steps (identify, codify, standardize, embed, supervise and learn), with clinician checkpoints placed where errors are costliest, and says AI should flag gray-area cases for a second look rather than decide them. Saxena, who with co-authors called this a "human-in-command approach" in a World Economic Forum piece, recommends starting with one high-volume workflow and tracking turnaround, reviewer agreement and appeal results.


Sources:

  • Turning Clinical Knowledge Into Consistent Healthcare Operations - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Arpan Saxena

item.title: AI Outlook For 2027: Top Four Trends To Watch
item.description:
Alionço, founder and CEO of Pipefy, predicts that in 2027 the limiting factor for AI will often be broken processes rather than model capability, and points to four trends: governance as the gate to high-value regulated work, orchestration of disconnected agents, demands for financial proof of value, and unit economics as costs grow. Alionço cites surveys including a Deloitte finding that just 21% of surveyed leaders described their agentic AI governance as mature, and a McKinsey finding that one in five organizations said AI operating costs already limited their use. With finance increasingly steering AI budgets, Alionço argues the technology "has graduated from capability to accountability."


Sources:

  • AI Outlook For 2027: Top Four Trends To Watch - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Alessio Alionco

item.title: It’s Time To Extend Collective Defense To Consumers
item.description:
Dhaval argues that while large companies harden their defenses, ordinary people face AI-driven attacks such as poisoned instruction files that hijack coding agents and cloned voices of loved ones, plus new exposure from shopping agents holding more access than they need, and nothing comparable protects them. Because antivirus software and firewalls look for malicious code rather than natural-language instructions, Dhaval proposes consumer Information Sharing and Analysis Centers, with ISPs, carriers, device makers and AI platforms as members and CISA as the federal partner, to turn household attack data into protective updates for gateways and phones. Dhaval also calls for least-privilege defaults in consumer AI tools and suggests leaders pass along steps such as keeping agents out of downloads folders and, as the FBI advises, putting smart devices on a guest network.


Sources:

  • It’s Time To Extend Collective Defense To Consumers - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Ravi Dhaval

item.title: AI's Hidden Cost: When Organizational Debt Comes Due
item.description:
Uram, COO and CTO of Allianz subsidiary Solvd Group, argues that AI is exposing "organizational debt": unclear ownership, duplicated processes, conflicting goals and inconsistent data that employees have long worked around through informal know-how. An AI agent can't rely on knowing whom to call or which number to trust, Uram writes, so weak data accountability, murky decision authority and clashing performance targets grow costlier once agents act at machine speed. Rather than redesigning everything first, Uram recommends starting with one significant end-to-end process and settling a single accountable owner, agreed data definitions, clear limits on what AI may execute and outcome-based measures before automating.


Sources:

  • AI's Hidden Cost: When Organizational Debt Comes Due - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Luboslava Uram

item.title: What Happens To Your Premium Domains When You Pass Away?
item.description:
Gargiulo, CEO of VPN.com, warns that owners of premium domains, some worth seven figures, often leave them out of estate planning, so heirs may not know what they own, what it is worth or how to keep registrations renewed. Gargiulo recommends inventorying and valuing domains now, documenting credentials and renewal obligations, and working with an estate attorney to settle who can access them. Because not every inherited domain should be sold, and some may be worth holding or keeping in business use, Gargiulo's advice is to "plan for the asset, not necessarily its sale."


Sources:

  • What Happens To Your Premium Domains When You Pass Away? - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Michael Gargiulo

item.title: The Next Great Infrastructure Reset
item.description:
Sarmey, founder of FutureProof CXO, argues that the next enterprise infrastructure reset may begin outside the data center, in submarine cables, substations, telecom corridors or satellite networks, as projected growth in data center electricity use, an estimated $6.7 trillion capital cycle and concentrated undersea connectivity deepen interdependencies. Because multiple clouds and facilities can share failure points in power, telecom and identity, Sarmey contends that "Redundancy isn't resilience" unless dependencies are mapped and recovery is tested. Sarmey's proposed discipline, Infrastructure-Consequence Economics, would judge investments on risk-adjusted cost per trusted business outcome rather than the lowest unit price.


Sources:

  • The Next Great Infrastructure Reset - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Rajjie Sarmey

item.title: How To Keep CRM And ERP Silos From Killing Operational Efficiency
item.description:
Grushai, CEO of Peeklogic, argues that, in Grushai's experience, most operational waste traces to CRM and ERP platforms such as Salesforce and NetSuite that were bought separately and never integrated, leaving staff to shuttle data by hand and producing duplicate records, conflicting customer views and disrupted invoicing. Grushai advises mapping processes like lead to cash and order to cash, starting small with quick wins, and choosing between point-to-point connectors, which can deliver in days or weeks, and slower middleware hubs suited to companies with many systems to link. Consolidating trusted data also readies a business for AI, Grushai writes, though not every system needs connecting, and the work should be driven by business owners who know "where their processes break down".


Sources:

  • How To Keep CRM And ERP Silos From Killing Operational Efficiency - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Sergii Grushai

item.title: How To Combine External And Proprietary Data Without Losing Control
item.description:
Members of Forbes Technology Council offer 17 approaches to blending outside data with proprietary records while keeping privacy and control, from Yardley Pohl's recommendation of clean rooms and federated queries to Will Conaway's case for federated learning across decentralized sources. Corey Ercanbrack of Vasion argues for fusing datasets only inside a single logged execution step, warning that "The riskiest thing in most architectures isn't the query", while Frederik Riskær Pedersen of Maplith says companies should map their own personal fields and linking keys before any join. Other contributors suggest a synthetic twin of proprietary data (Gayathri Kolandaisami), private set intersection to compare only overlapping records (Elton Chan) and a one-way door into an air-gapped system (Vivek Thomas).


Sources:

  • How To Combine External And Proprietary Data Without Losing Control - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Expert Panel, Forbes Technology Council

item.title: AI Raises The Stakes For Discovery Data
item.description:
Hersch, who leads corporate scientific research at Genedata, argues that as AI models trained on early discovery data increasingly shape candidate selection and other development decisions, pharma companies risk "validation debt" in the form of documentation and traceability gaps that grow harder and costlier to fix the longer they accumulate before data reaches regulated GxP environments. Hersch notes that the EU AI Act sets data governance and logging requirements for high-risk systems, so discovery data used to train or test such models may need defensible provenance, which spreadsheets, single-lab notebooks and ad hoc scripts often can't show under the ALCOA++ integrity framework regulators apply. Waiting can be expensive, Hersch writes, citing McKinsey's analysis that a one-month slip in filing for a $1 billion asset could wipe out roughly $60 million of net present value.


Sources:

  • AI Raises The Stakes For Discovery Data - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Jana Hersch

item.title: Small Businesses: AI Should Enable Team Collaboration, Not Siloed Work Gains
item.description:
Chang, general manager of ASUS North America, cites a March Goldman Sachs survey in which 93% of small businesses using AI in daily operations found it useful but only 14% had fully integrated it into core operations, a gap Chang suggests may partly reflect treating AI as a personal productivity tool. Because handoffs between people are often the slowest part of team work, Chang argues AI should manage shared workflows, pointing to McKinsey's estimate that collaborative use in human-centered workflows could unlock up to $2.9 trillion in economic value by 2030. Small, close-knit teams can often adopt new workflows within weeks, Chang writes, and should begin by mapping where work passes between people and deciding where human judgment should stay.


Sources:

  • Small Businesses: AI Should Enable Team Collaboration, Not Siloed Work Gains - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Shawn Chang

item.title: The GCC Evolution: Moving From Cost Arbitrage To Value-Creation Engines
item.description:
Chandra, CEO of Dotsquares, writes that India's Global Capability Centers are shifting from offshore cost-cutting toward strategic roles in product engineering, architectural governance and digital transformation, citing a U.K. travel client whose decade-old development contract grew into ownership of CRM architecture and round-the-clock customer support. Chandra points to EY India research finding attrition in Tier-2 tech hubs can run as much as 10 percentage points below Tier-1 metros, and Nasscom figures showing a 20% to 30% talent-cost advantage and real estate overheads up to 50% lower. To turn a GCC into a strategic hub, Chandra recommends bringing its leaders into sprint planning and design reviews from the outset, setting up centers of excellence, and committing to three to four hours a day of structured interaction across borders.


Sources:

  • The GCC Evolution: Moving From Cost Arbitrage To Value-Creation Engines - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Bankim Chandra

item.title: Turning Your Business Into An AI Lab Before Selling It To Clients
item.description:
Babkin of Azati describes spending three years turning the company into its own AI lab before pitching AI transformation to clients, including roughly 24 of 30 months that amounted to building "yet another CRM" and a favorite engineer-ranking feature, CV-Tinder, that almost nobody used. The turnaround came from moving AI into the work chats where staff already spend their day, and the resulting layer now gives each user a personal agent connected to billing, CRM, GitLab and other systems, with agents since October 2026 turning repeated tasks into reusable skills that a supervising agent reviews. Babkin's lessons include putting AI where people already ask questions, leaving decisions with legal or financial responsibility to a human, and recognizing that a release made for optics "costs you twice": once to build it and again to regain trust after it goes unused.


Sources:

  • Turning Your Business Into An AI Lab Before Selling It To Clients - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Andrew Babkin

item.title: Three Questions (And Answers) To Secure The AI-Enabled Workplace
item.description:
Danhieux, CEO of Secure Code Warrior, warns that AI adoption is "expanding faster than AI readiness" and notes that fewer than a quarter of senior business and technology leaders think their staff are fully ready, while nearly four in five expect AI's speed to outpace their governance. Drawing on a 2026 PagerDuty survey in which two-thirds of office professionals said they had used AI tools despite knowing policy forbade it and 88% had shared work information with public AI tools, Danhieux argues security leaders must learn who is using AI, what data employees hand it, and whether the company could prove responsible adoption to an auditor. Because bans rarely work, Danhieux recommends pairing governance with AI literacy aimed at changing behavior, such as asking whether an agent truly needs the access being granted.


Sources:

  • Three Questions (And Answers) To Secure The AI-Enabled Workplace - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Pieter Danhieux

item.title: Streaming’s Missed Opportunity: Being A Fan Is Getting More Expensive
item.description:
Lonstein, CEO of VFT Solutions, argues that pro sports show how streaming has missed its chance, citing Houlihan Lokey research that the NFL's yearly national media rights value climbed roughly 90% to $12.25 billion and the NBA's 159% to $6.9 billion, while fans juggle Sunday Ticket, League Pass, MLB.TV and other services, none of which guarantees every live game. Lonstein also points to Gametime resale data reported by Axios showing inflation-adjusted NFL resale ticket prices up 173% from 2015 to 2025, while conceding that rising rights fees aren't necessarily what drives ticket prices up. The danger, Lonstein writes, is that following a team becomes "a privilege rather than a shared experience" and streaming should be judged by whether fans can easily discover, reach and pay for what they love.


Sources:

  • Streaming’s Missed Opportunity: Being A Fan Is Getting More Expensive - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Wayne Lonstein

item.title: What Happens When Electronics Face The Real World? Precision Timing Holds The Key
item.description:
Lutz, a SiTime co-founder, uses the Bay Lights on the San Francisco–Oakland Bay Bridge, which went dark in early 2023 after traffic vibration, coastal weather and salt corrosion wore down its electronics, as a lesson that reliability depends on how devices hold up over years in the field rather than on the bench. Lutz argues that as systems shrink while deployments move to harsher edge settings such as EV drivetrains, remote communication towers and desert solar sites, resilience must be built into the architecture, and timing components are critical because their failures can cascade into data corruption or full breakdowns. Lutz urges engineers to set environmental assumptions at the start of development and to assess timing, power and thermal behavior together, and to qualify products against their full lifecycle.


Sources:

  • What Happens When Electronics Face The Real World? Precision Timing Holds The Key - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Markus Lutz

item.title: 18 Ways To Win Executive Buy-In For Technology Investments
item.description:
Forbes Technology Council members offer 18 ways to build the case for executive backing of technology spending, with Sergii Grushai of Peeklogic advising leaders to first show they use what they already pay for, noting that the Salesforce organizations Peeklogic audits typically use under 40% of their licensed features. Mayank Bhola of Testmu AI suggests stating the cost of inaction in numbers the CFO already tracks, while Jagadish Gokavarapu of Wissen Infotech recommends a map showing which approved projects would lose people or launch dates if the new investment took priority. Brandon Fuchs of Balenor Pharmaceuticals argues that a small pilot with real users reveals "whether anyone will do it" and that the pilot's usage curve belongs in the meeting before the demo.


Sources:

  • 18 Ways To Win Executive Buy-In For Technology Investments - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Expert Panel, Forbes Technology Council

item.title: Feeling Is The Human Superpower AI May Never Learn
item.description:
Peng argues that feeling, "the capacity for existence to matter to us", is humanity's deepest power, drawing on neuroscientist Antonio Damasio's view that feelings arise from the nervous system's bond with the body it regulates. Citing a September 2026 paper by Geoffrey Hinton and coauthors on a possible intelligence explosion, Peng contends that even far greater machine intelligence would not by itself show that an AI experiences anything, noting that researchers remain divided on whether consciousness depends on living systems. For AI builders, Peng says progress should mean giving people "more room to live", such as assistants that strengthen someone's relationships instead of making a product harder to quit.


Sources:

  • Feeling Is The Human Superpower AI May Never Learn - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Regan Peng

item.title: Rethinking How Teams Plan, Make Decisions And Work Together
item.description:
Gezgin, who became CEO of Eightpoint in July 2024, describes two years of bringing shared data, platform and design capabilities closer to product teams so departments stop tackling similar problems in isolation.
