Gezgin favors pairing steady annual goals with two-week sprints that test assumptions and wants leaders to own outcomes, explain their reasoning and flag issues early, in a culture where disappointing results can be talked about openly. As AI lets teams produce more, Gezgin argues progress should be judged by how quickly teams validate assumptions and apply lessons, noting that AI tools already help the desktop team automate testing and browser upgrades, though people still sign off on releases.


Sources:

  • Rethinking How Teams Plan, Make Decisions And Work Together - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Deniz Gezgin

item.title: The Cognitive Enterprise In 2027: Four Priorities For AI Maturity
item.description:
Kindiger, CEO of Droma, says AI is speeding up individual tasks while exposing how fragmented enterprise intelligence remains, pointing to a McKinsey article on its state of AI survey in which 80% of respondents reported better personal productivity but only 37% saw a positive effect on EBIT. Kindiger's answer is the cognitive enterprise, a framework IBM described in 2019, which would link sensing, institutional memory, judgment, governed action and learning so that a service disruption, for example, gets one coordinated response, with reversible fixes automated and consequential changes left for human approval. Leaders should start with a single cross-department workflow, set baselines and decide what AI may recommend, execute or escalate, since by 2027 maturity will hinge on whether the enterprise grows "more capable because of the work it has already done".


Sources:

  • The Cognitive Enterprise In 2027: Four Priorities For AI Maturity - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Casey Kindiger

item.title: AI Agents Are Only As Good As The Tools They Can Reach
item.description:
Artabane, SVP of product management at Auros, says Model Context Protocol support has become an expectation, with almost half of the technical leaders responding to a December 2025 Stacklok survey reporting MCP in production, so the real question is what agents can reach through it. Because agents can now squeeze a sprint's worth of building into an afternoon, Artabane argues customer feedback has to keep pace, and research-focused MCP servers let teams recruit participants and launch studies without leaving tools like Claude, ChatGPT and Figma Make; Auros's work with puppy-coaching app Zigzag on its Ziggy chat feature yielded a 96% positive rating and 27% fewer human trainer support requests in the first six months. Artabane cautions against relying only on synthetic users, since a model validating another model's output "may confirm what's typical and miss what's surprising."


Sources:

  • AI Agents Are Only As Good As The Tools They Can Reach - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Artabane

item.title: The Four Pillars Of Data Readiness For Agentic Commerce
item.description:
Yu, CEO of VGS, argues that agentic commerce is opening a data blind spot for merchants, who risk becoming "passive endpoints" in transactions they can't fully see. Yu's four pillars are telling legitimate shopping agents from malicious bots (Amazon currently blocks some AI platforms, and Mastercard has given the FIDO Alliance its verified intents framework), verifying the consumer behind an agent, sharing consumer mandates such as price ceilings, since an agent capped at $500 silently skips a $501 table, and payment credentials, because single-use agentic tokens can't support loyalty or card-on-file relationships. Calling these gaps design choices rather than inherent flaws, Yu urges merchants to join standards and protocol discussions now instead of inheriting an architecture built by others.


Sources:

  • The Four Pillars Of Data Readiness For Agentic Commerce - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Chuck Yu

item.title: Your Attacker's AI Knows You Better Than Yours Does
item.description:
Ritesh, founder and CEO of CYFIRMA, points to Japan's first cybersecurity state of emergency on Oct. 9, 2026, after ransomware at SoftBank-owned cloud provider IDC Frontier reached almost 500 client companies and local governments, and to an open-source AI agent's credential-stuffing campaign against seven South Korean banks and lenders. Ritesh argues AI has stripped away the language and skill barriers that once shielded both countries, producing "millions of good-enough attackers", yet the intrusions exploited ordinary weaknesses such as broken authorization, exposed admin APIs and flaws for which patches already existed. Rather than trying to out-model adversaries, Ritesh says defenders should start from their sector's real threats, gather outside-in data on what is being discussed, sold and scanned about them, and map attack paths, because AI is a multiplier and "multiplying zero still gives you zero."


Sources:

  • Your Attacker's AI Knows You Better Than Yours Does - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Kumar Ritesh

item.title: How To Make The Shift From Tech Executive To Board Director
item.description:
Ombach, a board member and Airbus senior vice president, writes that seasoned executives on deep-tech scale-up boards are tempted to fix problems themselves, but when a director begins running the work, it becomes less clear what the CEO is responsible for. Ombach recommends letting management explain its recommendation first, making clear whether a discussion is meant for advice, approval or a progress report, and wording questions so they don't sound like instructions, while still challenging plans that are incomplete. Before stepping in, Ombach suggests directors ask whether the matter belongs to the board, whether they are sharpening the decision or taking over the solution, and who owns the next step, and that they ask the CEO directly what help is needed.


Sources:

  • How To Make The Shift From Tech Executive To Board Director - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Greg Ombach

item.title: Your Holiday Fraud Rules May Be Turning Away Your Best New Customers
item.description:
Hamilton, CEO and co-founder of pmtbox, argues that merchants who tighten fraud rules before the holidays often reject good customers, because fraud usually shrinks as a share of transactions when legitimate volume surges, citing TransUnion's finding that 2.4% of U.S. online transactions over the 2023 Thanksgiving-to-Cyber Monday stretch were suspected fraud versus 4% for the rest of that year. False declines trigger none of the warnings chargebacks do (Datos Insights estimates the industry average at 1.51% of annual sales), and the gift buyers with mismatched shipping addresses or unusually large orders who trip stricter rules are often the new shoppers merchants paid to attract. Hamilton advises checking last year's holiday fraud rate before changing rules, setting a seasonal approval-rate target reviewed weekly, and not reacting mid-season to raw attempt counts.


Sources:

  • Your Holiday Fraud Rules May Be Turning Away Your Best New Customers - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Wayne Hamilton

item.title: The Endpoint: Where Security Breaches Still Thrive
item.description:
Greenway, CTO at 10ZiG, contends that endpoint security is losing ground to AI-focused detection even though endpoints remain among the most vulnerable targets, quoting Forrester senior analyst Paddy Harrington that agentic systems use the same identities and permissions as people, so "they inherit the same risks." Citing Verizon's 2026 DBIR, Greenway notes that exploiting vulnerabilities has become the top way attackers first get in, at 31%, while the share of critical vulnerabilities remediated dropped to 26% in 2025 from 38% the year before. Greenway argues for prevention through patching, tighter user privileges and authentication, and highlights thin clients running a purpose-built Linux OS that store no data locally and reboot to a clean state, noting they are a popular choice where devices are shared across shifts, as in healthcare and call centers.


Sources:

  • The Endpoint: Where Security Breaches Still Thrive - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Kevin Greenway

item.title: The Bedside Is A New Attack Surface: Securing Medical Devices In The Age Of AI
item.description:
Fractional vCISO Dan Sorensen argues that medical device security has become one of cybersecurity's most consequential areas, citing Claroty findings that 89% of 351 healthcare organizations had internet-exposed devices with vulnerabilities exploited in active ransomware campaigns. With more than a thousand FDA-authorized AI-enabled devices, he warns of threats such as data poisoning, model evasion and performance drift that traditional device security programs weren't built to catch. An attacker, he writes, could "quietly degrade the model so it misses a tumor" without anyone noticing for months.


Sources:

  • The Bedside Is A New Attack Surface: Securing Medical Devices In The Age Of AI - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Dan Sorensen

item.title: Beyond Good Intentions: Strong Algorithms, Weak Keys And The Assumptions AI Is Exposing
item.description:
Qrypt cofounder Denis Mandich says two October disclosures — Anthropic's reconstruction of how several NIST elliptic-curve seeds were generated and the discovery of weak private keys in internet trust infrastructure — show that familiar standards and trusted institutions aren't sufficient assurance on their own. He cautions that a mundane cause, like a deprecated random-number generator, explains how a result arose but not why it was chosen, since "apparent carelessness cannot, by itself, establish innocence." He urges security teams to use new AI tools to "trust but verify" their cryptographic foundations.


Sources:

  • Beyond Good Intentions: Strong Algorithms, Weak Keys And The Assumptions AI Is Exposing - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Denis Mandich

item.title: Securing The Modern Shop Floor: Why Cybersecurity Needs Operational Trust
item.description:
Claudio Laterreur argues that getting systems back online after a cyber incident doesn't prove operations are safe, and proposes operational trust — confidence that operations behave as intended and that recovery returns them to a verified, known-good state. He lists warning signals such as unauthorized setpoint changes, abnormal machine behavior and quality drift, noting each could also stem from maintenance, sensor errors or human mistakes. Four tests — business exposure, approved tolerance, operating explanation and cyber pathway — help leaders decide when to escalate a joint cyber and operations investigation.


Sources:

  • Securing The Modern Shop Floor: Why Cybersecurity Needs Operational Trust - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Claudio Laterreur

item.title: Your AI Agents Need Performance Reviews, Too
item.description:
Hack The Box CEO Haris Pylarinos recounts an AI coding agent that deleted his personal project's production database overnight, noting that "being honest about destroying a database doesn't undo the damage." He argues agents need ongoing evaluations much like employees, because their behavior can shift as models and inputs change, and should arguably be held to a higher standard than humans. Leaders should define each agent's tasks, permitted decisions, system access and escalation conditions, then assess accuracy, repeatability, scope discipline and recovery when things go wrong.


Sources:

  • Your AI Agents Need Performance Reviews, Too - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Haris Pylarinos

item.title: How Physical AI Will Make The Network Part Of The Machine
item.description:
Lancesoft's Venkatesh Gokulraju envisions networks that don't just carry data for robots and autonomous machines but help them sense, decide and act, picturing an airfield baggage tractor that keeps working through satellite-navigation interference. Physical AI, he writes, scores networks on "whether the right decision arrives while it still applies," splitting intelligence across machine, edge and cloud or satellite layers. He expects radio sites to become AI sites, the edge to become a decision layer and determinism to become a product, with many of the hardest hurdles being organizational.


Sources:

  • How Physical AI Will Make The Network Part Of The Machine - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Venkatesh Gokulraju

item.title: Where To Draw The Line On Agentic AI's Autonomy
item.description:
rSTAR's Vivek Ahuja says enterprises should set autonomy limits for each action an AI agent takes rather than for the agent as a whole, citing Deloitte research that close to three-quarters of companies plan to deploy agentic AI within two years while only 21% have a mature governance model. He suggests asking what happens if the agent errs, whether the action can be reversed and whether it affects a customer's rights, safety or finances, then sorting actions into acting independently, preparing for approval, or stopping and escalating. Those boundaries, he writes, should be enforced through system permissions, transaction limits and approval controls.


Sources:

  • Where To Draw The Line On Agentic AI's Autonomy - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Vivek Ahuja

item.title: An AI Kill Switch Is A Comforting Illusion
item.description:
Mindgard's Peter Garraghan argues that the AI kill switch debated in Congress amounts to existing operational controls — stopping inference, cutting access and rolling back — and that calling it an AI kill switch "is just marketing." The hard part is deciding what should trigger it, since most AI failures such as model drift and slow data leakage are quiet, and a switch waiting on a human engages only after the damage is done. He urges defense-in-depth through threat modeling, red teaming and continuous monitoring, keeping the kill switch as a last line of defense.


Sources:

  • An AI Kill Switch Is A Comforting Illusion - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Peter Garraghan

item.title: The Race To Produce Ads Faster Is A Race Toward The Middle
item.description:
Predis.ai cofounder Tanmay Ratnaparkhe argues that generative tools have made ad production so fast that speed is now a baseline rather than an advantage, since competitors use the same tools. Because the models gravitate toward what is statistically likely, he says the race pushes everyone toward the middle, citing a 2026 meta-analysis that found a small but significant homogenization effect, and faster iteration "only gets you there faster." The scarce skill now is judging which of many options deserves a real budget and being able to justify that choice.


Sources:

  • The Race To Produce Ads Faster Is A Race Toward The Middle - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Tanmay Ratnaparkhe

item.title: Application Bloat Is An Emergency Waiting To Happen
item.description:
Jason Rose describes a hospital IT leader who renewed a six-figure application contract just as the parent health system bought a different platform for the same function, an example of duplicated software spending he says costs health systems more than they realize. He recommends an application portfolio modernization analysis, using tools such as Gartner's TIME framework, to find overlapping systems, measure what they cost and pick which should become the standard. A 2026 CHIME survey found 76% of CIOs call application rationalization critical, but only one in five have a fully implemented program.


Sources:

  • Application Bloat Is An Emergency Waiting To Happen - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Jason Rose

item.title: 19 Ways To Rethink Network Design For Distributed Workloads
item.description:
Forbes Technology Council members list network-design assumptions that break down once workloads span cloud, edge and on-premises sites, starting with SecureX's Victor Cardona arguing that security should track identity and applications instead of location. Emma McGrattan of Actian offers a simple test — "If connectivity to the cloud disappears, what stops working?" — while EE Solutions' Nicholas Domnisch warns that two carriers can still share one conduit, so a single construction accident could cut both links. Other tips include Akhilesh Sharma's call to engineer for traffic bursts rather than averages and Nikhil Jathar's advice to count round trips in a transaction before paying for more bandwidth.


Sources:

  • 19 Ways To Rethink Network Design For Distributed Workloads - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Expert Panel, Forbes Technology Council

item.title: High Agency Matters More
item.description:
As AI agents take over more execution, Cerebrum Tech's Erdem Erkul argues, citing Andrej Karpathy, that the harder-to-find human trait is agency: owning a problem, taking a first small step and answering for the outcome. Erkul cites an MIT experiment with more than 2,200 people in which AI users produced 50% more ads with stronger scripts, yet human teams made better visuals and the AI-assisted ads looked more alike. Leaders, Erkul writes, should focus on the right problems, scrutinize AI output and protect accountability, since "A decision made with AI is still a human decision" that someone must answer for.


Sources:

  • High Agency Matters More - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Erdem Erkul

item.title: T+1 And The Global Race To Build The Next Generation Of Market Infrastructure
item.description:
With U.K. and EU securities markets moving to T+1 settlement in October 2027, Tokenovate CEO Richard Baker cites Censuswide research for the firm showing 83% of U.K. post-trade professionals expect to hit the deadline but only 32% say they are fully prepared now. Baker points to the U.S. shift, where same-day affirmation rose to almost 95% of transactions, but cites the U.K.'s Investment Association as noting that some U.S. firms leaned on added headcount and manual work-arounds that have proved hard to unwind. Baker argues that shared standards like the FINOS Common Domain Model and interoperable automation built now would also position markets for tokenized assets and the widespread T+0 or atomic settlement that Tokenovate's research suggests the industry anticipates within 3.7 years.


Sources:

  • T+1 And The Global Race To Build The Next Generation Of Market Infrastructure - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Richard Baker

item.title: Why Personal Agents Don’t Belong In The Enterprise (Yet)
item.description:
Globality CTO Keith McFarlane argues that always-on personal agents such as Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots are impressive but not ready for corporate use, since they lack certifications like SOC 2 and ISO 27001 and would turn into data subprocessors once connected to work systems. McFarlane also flags cost, noting reports that Uber exhausted its 2026 AI coding budget by April and that agents running unattended "will consume far more" than prompt-driven tools. Enterprise agents in governed areas such as procurement, with guardrails, logged actions and human escalation, will instead grow more personal over time, McFarlane predicts.


Sources:

  • Why Personal Agents Don’t Belong In The Enterprise (Yet) - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Keith McFarlane

item.title: Why Frontier AI Raises The Standard For Software Assurance
item.description:
RevEng.AI founder James Patrick-Evans argues that frontier AI is turning reverse engineering of compiled software, once a weeks-to-months effort per application, into something practical at scale, with models that can reconstruct source and flag risky behavior straight from binaries. The need is growing, Patrick-Evans writes, because supply chains lean heavily on outside code — JPMorgan estimates 77% is reused dependencies — and AI coding agents are adding code at machine speed. Patrick-Evans calls binary analysis a complement to SAST and DAST rather than a replacement, cautions that AI findings still need validation, and says customers and regulators will come to expect this deeper assurance.


Sources:

  • Why Frontier AI Raises The Standard For Software Assurance - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: James Patrick-Evans

item.title: We Are Asking The Wrong Question About AI Agent Security
item.description:
Britive CEO Art Poghosyan says the key question about AI agents is not whether to allow them but what each one may do, and why, citing Gartner's projection that the average global Fortune 500 enterprise will run more than 150,000 agents by 2028 while only 13% of organizations feel their agent governance is adequate. Poghosyan warns that standing privileges and checkout-style just-in-time access leave reusable rights behind, and that killing an agent's process "doesn't revoke the authority" if its credentials stay valid. The fix, Poghosyan argues, is access created per task, checked action by action and removed afterward, alongside an inventory of every agent and its accountable owner.


Sources:

  • We Are Asking The Wrong Question About AI Agent Security - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Artyom Poghosyan

item.title: How Banks Can Govern Customer-Owned AI Agents They Don’t Own
item.description:
OvationCXM CEO Alfred Kahn argues that AI agents run by business clients are becoming a new banking channel that current controls, built for portal users or preapproved system links, cannot govern. Kahn's company surveyed 520 U.S. finance leaders and found 75% using or piloting agents, with 54% of agent users saying they would find a workaround if their bank could not support them. Kahn recommends separating tool discovery via MCP from authorization in a bank-side control plane, exposing narrow business tasks instead of raw APIs, registering each agent with its own credentials and rolling out read-only uses before money movement.


Sources:

  • How Banks Can Govern Customer-Owned AI Agents They Don’t Own - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Alfred Kahn

item.title: Why Context Is Capital In Enterprise AI
item.description:
EXL chief AI officer Anand Logani argues that as models improve and get cheaper, companies should effectively rent their models and treat their own decision records, ontologies and institutional know-how as an appreciating asset Logani calls context capital. Pointing to McKinsey's estimate that only 37% of businesses can tie enterprise-level financial impact to AI, Logani says pilots stall on edge cases needing knowledge no LLM has, such as which specialist can find a missing accident report. Logani describes separate build and serving paths for a context graph and urges leaders to check whether the context their AI tools gather is contractually their own.


Sources:

  • Why Context Is Capital In Enterprise AI - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Anand Logani

item.title: Where Human Judgment Belongs In AI Workflows
item.description:
Evaila's Emily Lewis-Pinnell draws on a Stanford analysis of 249,834 Claude conversations, which found 56% of actionable tasks were consequential and that users engaged more as stakes rose, to argue that being fluent with AI means knowing when to challenge or check an answer. Lewis-Pinnell pairs it with a Stanford Digital Economy Lab finding that escalation-based deployments were associated with median productivity gains of 71% versus 30% for approve-every-output models, while noting the comparison does not prove causation. Lewis-Pinnell's advice is to scale human review to what is at stake in the work, teach people to evaluate flawed outputs, spell out decision rights and make clear that challenging AI is expected.


Sources:

  • Where Human Judgment Belongs In AI Workflows - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Emily Lewis-Pinnell

item.title: Your Website Works For Humans, But Does It Work For AI Agents?
item.description:
ILoveMyQA.com founder Margarita Simonova warns that a checkout flow can pass human QA and still trip up an AI assistant that cannot tell which button adds an item to the cart or misreads poorly labeled options, so the site works while the task fails. Simonova says good accessibility practices help agents but are not the same as agent compatibility, so teams should test whole tasks, such as booking a refundable hotel stay within budget, and check whether the agent caught fees and conditions. Businesses should also decide which actions agents may take and require confirmation for consequential ones, without stripping out fraud protections, Simonova writes.


Sources:

  • Your Website Works For Humans, But Does It Work For AI Agents? - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Margarita Simonova
